papers.title: A data-driven approach for learning traffic assignment using an artificial neural network
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers - Transport
papers.abstract: Solving transportation network design problems using traffic assignment models becomes increasingly impractical as the size of the considered network grows, due to the need to evaluate numerous candidate solutions. This study aims to model the traffic assignment process through a data-driven approach, and introduces a model based on an artificial neural network (ANN) to predict the total travel time in a network under various link capacity modifications for a specified set of links. ANN-based prediction models are trained and validated on a synthetic data set generated from a medium-sized network to evaluate the feasibility of the proposed approach. Models developed using different ANN architectures highlight the importance of selecting the most suitable architecture specific to the problem. The practical value of the ANN-based prediction model becomes apparent when used in optimising a transportation network design problem instead of the traditional traffic-assignment model: the ANN-based model reduced by up to 60 000 times the computation time required for the optimisation.

papers.title: Toward Lifecycle-Ready Digital Twins For Facility Technical Management
papers.abstract: Digital twins are increasingly promoted as a means to address persistent challenges in the built environment, yet their role in maintenance-focused facility management (FM) remains underexplored. This article explores the practical integration of digital twins into facility technical management through a real-life case environment involving three operational buildings and a two-year deployment period. Using a mixed-method approach combining surveys, interviews, operational observations, and industry feedback, the study investigates the organizational, technical, and information-management-related factors affecting the implementation and usability of BIM-based digital twins in maintenance operations.The findings identify key requirements related to BIM data structures, information management practices, naming conventions, and the involvement of maintenance stakeholders during the design and handover phases. Based on the case findings, the article outlines a four-step BIM process development framework and a four-step BIM enablement framework for facility technical management.The study further highlights the importance of user-friendly graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in bridging the gap between design-oriented BIM environments and the practical needs of maintenance personnel. The findings suggest that digital twins should be approached as continuously managed lifecycle information assets rather than static handover deliverables. The article contributes practice-oriented insights into how BIM-based digital twins can support information continuity and operational usability in facility technical management contexts.

papers.title: A Digital Twin–Based Simulation Framework for Safe Curve Speed Estimation Using Unity
papers.journal: Transportation Research Record Journal of the Transportation Research Board
papers.abstract: Horizontal curves are often associated with roadway crashes because of speed misjudgment and loss of control. With the growing adoption of connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs), the accurate estimation of safe speed at curves is becoming increasingly important. The widely used AASHTO design method for safe curve speed estimation relies on an analytical equation based on a simplified point mass model, which often uses conservative parameters to account for vehicular and environmental variations. This paper presents a digital twin–based framework for estimating safe speed at curves using a physics-driven virtual environment developed in the Unity engine. In this framework, a real-world horizontal road curve is selected, and vehicle speed data are collected using a radar gun under various weather conditions. A 3-D model of the road curve is constructed in a Unity environment using roadway geometric and elevation data. A parameterized vehicle model is integrated, allowing for variations in mass, acceleration, and center of gravity to reflect different vehicle types and loading scenarios. The simulation identifies the maximum safe speed at which a vehicle can traverse the given curve, providing a more vehicle- and environment-specific estimate of the safe operating speed. The study validated that the safe curve speed estimates generated by the simulation were consistent with the real-world speed values observed at the curve. This study demonstrates how a physics-based digital twin can estimate a safer and more adaptive operating speed for vehicles traversing horizontal curves.

papers.title: A unified framework for global indoor air quality: transitioning from guidelines to actionable open regulatory standards
papers.abstract: Indoor air quality (IAQ) is a global public health issue that affects people regardless of age, geography, or socioeconomic status. Today, no single cohesive global IAQ standard exists. Despite the United Nations (UN) declaration of human rights to clean air (2022) current guidelines vary widely, leaving governments, industry, building managers, and residents without consistent, actionable benchmarks. A unified framework is proposed by the organization Global Open Air Quality Standards (GO AQS) in this paper for an IAQ regulatory pathway which is called Global Open Indoor Air Quality Standards (GO IAQS). Although the World Health Organization (WHO) has maintained since 1987 guidelines that outdoor standards apply indoors, the most prominent air quality targets focus on ambient pollutants due to a relative lack of indoor data; consequently, these existing frameworks can be insufficient for indoor environments where unique factors, such as the accumulation of human breath, require additional parameters like carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) to serve as markers for ventilation. Fragmented and poorly designed indoor environmental standards often focus on upstream determinants of IAQ, such as ventilation rates, which are challenging to measure, especially if buildings are ventilated naturally, and lack clarity for the public. In contrast, parameters such as CO 2 and fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) have been used as accessible metrics for the hundreds of thousands of low-cost monitors globally. Furthermore, outdoor-centric standards rely on long-term averaging windows (e.g., annual or daily limits) primarily intended for high-level planning to manage long-term health risks and drive systemic, year-over-year improvements in air quality. When applied to indoor monitors, these are frequently misinterpreted as real-time ceiling limits. This framework advocates for a strategic shift toward shorter averaging windows and thresholds to safeguard the public indoors. Thresholds are proposed as action levels that trigger immediate responses, such as increasing ventilation, to protect health. We argue that a universal, open-source IAQ standard and index are needed to provide standardized breakpoints for air quality monitors, similar to the outdoor air quality index (AQI). This transparent, expert-informed initiative can provide policymakers with the regulatory clarity required to protect populations from acute and chronic health impacts and is expected to enhance resilience against indoor chemical hazards and airborne diseases.

papers.title: A Comparative Analysis of the Seismic Performance of Four Buildings Representative of Bagan’s Monumental Heritage
papers.abstract: This paper presents the outcomes of nonlinear static pushover and time history analyses, using both recorded and simulated ground motion signals, on 3D finite element macro-models of four buildings representative of Bagan’s monumental heritage: Myin-pya-gu (1493), Zan-thi (east) (558), Tha-mu-ti-hpaya (844), and Kya-zin-hpaya (1219). The simulations are validated against the observed seismic damage in the 1975 and 2016 earthquakes. The results of the nonlinear finite element method (NLFEM) analyses are complemented by seismic rocking analysis conducted on nonstructural elements, such as spires, through nonlinear kinematic analysis. Analytical estimates of acceleration levels capable of causing shear failure in spires are provided, focusing on elements with a slenderness ratio that makes them vulnerable to shearing rather than rocking (i.e. flexure-controlled) failure modes. A comparative assessment of seismic performance is presented for the four buildings, highlighting the influence of plan symmetry and vertical continuity. These attributes are proposed as key criteria for selecting appropriate retrofit schemes to protect Bagan’s monuments against future seismic events.

papers.title: Beam layout design in shear wall structures using a diffusion model guided by rule-based masks
papers.abstract: Serving as critical load supports and transfer components in shear wall structures, beams require layout designs that balance mechanical rationality with architectural functionality constraints. Conventional design methods, which rely on engineers' expertise, are challenging to systematize and are inherently inefficient. Moreover, existing intelligent design algorithms have attempted to integrate constraints related to architectural space and mechanical topology while delivering sufficiently detailed outputs, ultimately resulting in suboptimal outcomes. To address these challenges, this study synthesizes engineering experience rules pertaining to spatial functionality and load-bearing constraints and encodes them into a mask that delineates potential beam placement locations on a building plan. Subsequently, a diffusion model, well-known for its ability to generate intricate design details, is employed to produce the corresponding beam layout from the image mask. This approach, designated as the mask-constrained diffusion model for beam layout design in shear wall structures, introduces a key innovation: mitigating the uncontrolled generative range typically associated with diffusion models during beam layout configuration. By embedding engineering knowledge into a mask that constrains the diffusion process, the generation boundaries are effectively regulated, ensuring controllable and effective design outcomes. Analysis indicates that the designs produced by the mask-constrained diffusion model surpass the quality of existing intelligent design methods, achieving a relative 35.0% improvement in consistency with engineer-generated designs while concurrently satisfying critical mechanical performance criteria. This study provides a novel perspective on the intelligent design of beam layouts and serves as a valuable reference for the application of diffusion models in the structural design of buildings.

papers.title: System dynamic model on cost-time-material waste analysis for supply chain management of offsite panelised systems in the housing sector
papers.abstract: Purpose To effectively support the housing sector, the offsite construction (OSC) supply chain (SC) requires strengthened skills, expanded operational capacity and improved organisational capabilities. However, ongoing SC management (SCM) issues, such as cost overruns, inefficient processes and material waste, continue to limit the housing sector’s adoption of OSC. By addressing these barriers, this study aims to improve OSC-SCM processes while expanding the talent and capability base needed for construction ecosystems. Design/methodology/approach A system dynamics (SD) modelling approach is used to analyse cost and time dynamics under multiple disruption scenarios quantitatively. The model incorporates key barriers, like design inefficiencies, labour shortages, equipment delays and logistical constraints, while also simulating the potential performance gains achievable through skill development, capacity expansion and capability upgrading. Findings The simulation results demonstrate the complex relationships among SC performance, operational capacity and personnel capability in OSC. The findings point to key areas for leverage where focused interventions, such as digital design integration, improved worker training and rapid logistics planning, can increase productivity, cut waste and improve preparedness simultaneously. Originality/value In the OSC context, this research presents a novel integration of SD modelling, showing how digitally driven skill enhancement and capacity building can serve as catalysts for attaining next-generation construction performance and overcoming enduring SCM barriers.

papers.title: Delay-Compensated MPC for Path Tracking of Articulated Steering Vehicles
papers.journal: Journal of Transportation Engineering Part A Systems
papers.abstract: Abstract Articulated steering vehicles are key equipment for mining transportation, underground roadways, and heavy-duty material handling infrastructure, where insufficient path-tracking accuracy may reduce roadway safety margins and increase the risk of lane encroachment, collision, and traffic interruption in confined haulage corridors. Hydraulic actuator delay is a practical source of steering lag in such vehicles, but it is often simplified or neglected in existing path-tracking control studies. To address this gap, this study develops a delay-compensated model predictive control (MPC) framework by incorporating experimentally identified hydraulic actuator delay into the pre‍dictive control model. Simulation results showed that MPC provided better stability performance than linear quadratic regulator (LQR), reducing sideslip angle, yaw rate, and lateral acceleration by 21%–48% under representative lane-change maneuvers. With actuator-delay compensation, the proposed MPC further reduced the tractor lateral deviation by 53.12% under single lane change (SLC) and 83.63% under double lane change (DLC) conditions. These results indicate that the proposed method can improve the operational safety, tracking reliability, and automation readiness of articulated vehicles used in mining and infrastructure transportation scenarios.

papers.title: Satellite based multi-scale remote sensing system for infrastructure stability monitoring around an urban metro
papers.abstract: Ground settlement around urban metro systems can result from coupled interactions among wide-area surface displacement, local surface geometry, shallow subsurface conditions, and underground structural deformation. However, a single monitoring technique is insufficient to screen settlement-prone sections along long metro corridors and to interpret the associated surface and underground conditions at the selected site. This study proposes a multi-scale remote sensing system (MSRS) integrating InSAR, laser scanning, GPR, and BOTDR-based distributed fiber optic sensing for infrastructure stability monitoring around an urban metro ventilation facility. First, SBAS-InSAR analysis was performed along the approximately 16 km Bundang Line corridor between Suseo Station and Cheongnyangni Station in Seoul, Korea, to detect long-term LOS displacement tendencies. The corridor is a densely built urban area in which the alignment runs beneath paved arterial roads, and the target ventilation facility lies less than 10 m below ground surface. Based on the InSAR screening result, a ventilation facility near Gangnam-gu Office Station, where a relatively distinct settlement tendency was identified, was selected as the local target site. Ground-surface laser scanning was then used to resolve the present geometry of the localized surface depression around the ventilation facility, while GPR was applied to investigate pavement-layer thickness variations and localized reflection anomalies beneath the settlement area. Inside the ventilation chamber, underground laser scanning and BOTDR-based DFOS were used to evaluate the structural deformation. The temperature-corrected BOTDR result showed strain values ranging from approximately − 250 to + 350 με, with the maximum near 170–178 m and a second localized increase between 117 and 124 m, where a ceiling crack was mapped during the field inspection. These results indicate that the proposed MSRS can effectively screen settlement-prone sections along urban metro corridors and support staged interpretation of surface deformation, shallow subsurface conditions, and underground structural responses.

papers.title: A kinematically-constrained Hankel dynamic mode decomposition for short-term prediction of ship manoeuvring in ambient currents
papers.abstract: The accurate prediction of vessel manoeuvring dynamics is essential for ensuring navigational safety in the transition toward maritime autonomy. In this study, a kinematically-constrained Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (Hankel-DMD) approach is developed to model and predict vessel manoeuvring dynamics. The vessel motion is represented using a state formulation consisting of position and resultant speed, and the Hankel-DMD method, together with a component-wise normalisation of the position states, is used to extract the modes governing the system dynamics. To improve the physical consistency of the prediction, a kinematic constraint linking vessel position and speed is incorporated as a post-processing reconstruction step. The developed approach is examined using the data generated from a physics-based Maneuvering Modelling Group (MMG) manoeuvring model for an azimuth thruster-equipped tug. Three cases are considered, including manoeuvring in calm water, in the presence of ambient current along the X -direction (following), and current along the Y -direction (cross). Quantitative error metrics show that the kinematically-constrained reconstruction reduces the trajectory RMSE by 71% in calm water (from 1.09 m to 0.31 m) and by 60% for the following current (from 7.31 m to 2.90 m). For the cross current, however, the XY-normalised pure Hankel-DMD prediction achieves the slightly lower RMSE (1.34 m versus 2.80 m for the constrained reconstruction), indicating that the benefit of the kinematic constraint is scenario-dependent. These findings demonstrate that incorporating a kinematic constraint can improve the robustness of data-driven vessel trajectory prediction, although its benefit is case-dependent under environmental disturbances.

papers.title: Automated Roadside Vegetation Management Using LiDAR-Based Geospatial Simulations
papers.journal: Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering
papers.abstract: Abstract Effective roadside vegetation management is vital for safety, visibility, and infrastructure longevity. Traditional methods are often labor-intensive, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. This paper presents a novel approach leveraging light detection and ranging (LiDAR) data and geospatial analysis for large-scale roadside vegetation management. We introduce the vegetation-free volume (VFV), a spatial boundary defining clear roadside space. Using high-resolution LiDAR point clouds and advanced geospatial processing, we detect and quantify overgrown vegetation encroaching into the VFV. The method transforms point clouds into a homogeneous coordinate system, applies geometric queries to identify breaches, and generates horizontal and vertical density profiles to visualize overgrowth. Structured machine- and human-readable reports provide actionable insights for automated systems and field crews. Furthermore, we simulate vegetation growth and pruning cycles at the LiDAR-point level to support maintenance scheduling and resource optimization. Results demonstrated that integrating LiDAR and geospatial analysis enhances precision, efficiency, and scalability in roadside vegetation management.
